name: Deepfake Celebrity Endorsement Ads
summary: AI-generated video of a well-known South African business figure or broadcaster appears to endorse a trading platform that does not exist.

typicalLoss.note: The minimum deposit is usually pitched at around R4 000 to R5 000, then escalated by a 'personal account manager'.

targets: Social media users of every age
People who trust established local business figures

howItWorks.step: A face you trust, saying words they never said
howItWorks.detail: Video of prominent South African business people, broadcasters and news anchors is cloned with AI. Voice and lip movement are convincing on a phone screen.
The ad leads to a page styled as a real news publication, complete with masthead, bylines and comment sections, all fabricated.
The pitch is a small starting deposit and a state-backed or bank-backed 'wealth programme'. The low figure removes hesitation.
Within minutes of registering, a professional caller takes over. From here it becomes a standard fake trading platform with a rising dashboard and a withdrawal wall.

redFlags: A celebrity or public figure endorsing a specific trading platform in a social media ad. Real endorsements do not run this way.
A 'news article' whose links all lead to the same signup form.
Claims of government, Reserve Bank or major bank backing for a private trading scheme.
You are phoned within minutes of registering, by someone very good at their job.
The platform is not on the FSCA register.
illustrativeCase: A Facebook video shows a widely recognised South African businessman apparently telling an interviewer about an automated trading programme available to citizens for a R4 800 minimum. The clip is AI-generated; the interview never happened. A viewer registers, is called within four minutes by an articulate 'senior analyst', and over six weeks deposits R310 000.
howToProtect: Treat every celebrity investment endorsement in a social feed as fake by default. Prominent South Africans have publicly disclaimed these ads repeatedly.
Check the FSCA register before depositing anything, without exception.
Look at the video closely: hands, teeth, blinking and the edges of the jaw are still where AI generation breaks down.
Search the person's name plus 'deepfake' or 'scam warning'. The disclaimers are usually easy to find.
Never accept investment guidance from someone who phoned you.
ifYouveBeenHit: Stop depositing and refuse to pay any withdrawal fee.
Report to the FSCA, the SAPS, and your bank.
Report the advert to the platform and to the impersonated person's organisation.
Preserve screenshots, the platform URL and all transfer records.
Reject all recovery offers that follow.

faqs.q: Would Facebook allow a fraudulent ad using a real person's face?
faqs.a: It happens constantly. Ad review is largely automated, fraudulent advertisers rotate accounts rapidly, and removal usually comes after the campaign has already run.

faqs.q: The article was on a site that looked like a real newspaper.
faqs.a: It was a copy. Check the domain against the publication's real address, and try clicking a headline that is not part of the pitch. On a fake, nothing else works.
